title: Genesis
description: This ceramic vessel by Dimitria Barrows reinterprets the Genesis narrative through crypto ideology, transforming the Garden of Eden's temptation into a contemporary memento mori shaped from clay—as Adam himself was formed. The handmade vase depicts Adam and Eve reaching for the forbidden fruit beneath the Tree of Knowledge, with Pepe as the sly serpent between them. On the reverse, a Baroque-style inscription reads, "Don't Trust, Verify," linking the biblical theme of deception to the logic of blockchain. What once adorned sacred interiors becomes a reflection on trust in an age of immutable ledgers, collapsing scripture and crypto into a shared story of temptation and doubt.

title: This Is Fine
description: Adapted from This Is Fine (2013) by KC Green, this ceramic sculpture by Dimitria Barrows transforms the iconic internet meme into a contemporary memento mori. The handmade glazed vase depicts the calm dog amid flames on one side and his skeletal form on the other, offering a Baroque-like reflection on humor, denial, and decay. A crown of hand-sculpted roses and sharp thorns rises from the burnt rim, merging beauty and pain while evoking the vanitas tradition. Drawing on both internet culture and historical ceramic craftsmanship, Barrows combines Baroque aesthetics with the tactile ritual of clay. What once circulated online becomes a physical object that reflects on fragility in an age of digital permanence, asking what remains when the fire becomes our new normal.

title: The Year Is 2030
description: In THE YEAR IS 2030 Dimitria Barrows transforms the ceramic vessel into a rotating narrative surface where meme culture, cryptocurrency fantasy, and pop nostalgia converge. The composition unfolds as the viewer circles the form, activating it as both object and image. Five walking Pepe figures move in a rhythmic procession around the vessel, referencing the Grateful Dead's Dancing Bears. Their repetition suggests collectivity and speculative movement toward a promised digital future. Set within a bright pastoral landscape beneath a rainbow sky, the scene hovers between utopian sincerity and satire. Flowers and bees with Pepe faces extend the memetic landscape, while a painted pizza box nods to the first Bitcoin transaction. By translating internet imagery into hand-built ceramic, Barrows gives physical form to digital mythologies. The painted text reads: "THE YEAR IS 2030. YOU GLANCE AT YOUR BITCOIN WALLET AND IT DISPLAYS AN ASTRONOMICAL VALUE. YOU GRIN AND GO BACK TO YOUR BUSY DAY." The statement frames extreme digital wealth as everyday normality, capturing the quiet absurdity of Bitcoin futurism.

title: GM
description: This brightly glazed ceramic vessel brings together internet meme culture and cryptocurrency. On one side, a Salt Bae–like Pepe scatters BTC and Pepe tokens instead of salt, turning a familiar viral gesture into a playful reflection on hype, value, and online speculation. On the reverse, a red "GM" fries carton reveals a small Pepe tucked inside a McDonald's meal, nodding to hustle culture and the downturns of the crypto bear market.

title: CREAM
description: This handmade ceramic vase by contemporary artist Dimitria Barrows fuses classical porcelain motifs, animation history, and hip-hop culture into a visual allegory of money and ambition. Around the rim, the phrase "C.R.E.A.M."—short for "Cash Rules Everything Around Me"—references Wu-Tang Clan's financial mantra, played out through Tom and Jerry chasing each other across the vessel's surface. On one side, Jerry spears a wedge of cheese placed on a Ming-style porcelain plate, merging imperial ceramic symbolism with pop culture. The reverse shows Tom pushing an empty barrel, turning the cartoon rivalry into a metaphor for labor, desire, and lack. Blending slapstick, Chinese ceramic tradition, and hip-hop commentary, Barrows offers a pointed reflection on how ideas of value circulate across time and culture.

title: Homer
description: In Homer, Dimitria Barrows transforms a viral internet GIF from The Simpsons into a sculptural ceramic vessel. The work references the widely circulated image of Homer Simpson disappearing into a hedge—an enduring meme symbolizing social withdrawal, awkwardness, and digital-era self-erasure. The cylindrical form is fully encrusted with individually handmade ceramic leaves, glazed in layered greens and carved with detailed veining. From within this dense foliage, the cartoon figure emerges mid-disappearance, creating a visual tension between flat, digital animation and tactile, hand-built clay. The labor-intensive surface contrasts with the immediacy of meme culture, translating a looping digital image into a singular, materially grounded artwork. Open and hollow, the vessel reinforces themes of concealment and absence. By merging contemporary internet culture with traditional ceramic techniques, Barrows bridges digital and physical realms, situating meme imagery within the lineage of contemporary ceramic sculpture.

title: Magic Internet Money
description: This hand-painted ceramic vase by contemporary artist Dimitria Barrows explores the mythology and mechanics of cryptocurrency. The phrase "Magic Internet Money"—a meme used to describe Bitcoin—anchors the work's tension between effortless digital wealth and the intricate mathematics behind blockchain. At its center, Wizard Pepe conjures the blockchain in warm amber glaze. Floating equations—elliptic curves, hash functions, the whole arcane apparatus—orbit the wizard who sparked a thousand memes. Around the vessel, hand-painted cryptographic formulas reference SHA‑256 algorithms, block structures, and digital signatures, revealing the dense logic beneath crypto's playful surface. Rendered in a bright orange glaze referencing Bitcoin's color, the vase merges symbols of stored value with modern systems of speculative exchange. By blending meme culture, cryptography, and craft, Barrows exposes the paradox of "magic internet money"—a digital illusion built on immense computational labor.

title: SEEDPHRASE
description: Never share your seed phrase—not with your bank, not with an exchange, and not with a helpful DM. In this ceramic vessel, Dimitria Barrows reworks a scene from The Simpsons, replacing Springfield Elementary with "Blockchain Elementary School" and altering the billboard to read: "Send me your seedphrase." Rendered in ceramic, the image gains a sense of permanence, contrasting with the speed and disposability of digital fraud.

title: Buy the Dip
description: In Buy the Dip, Dimitria Barrows merges ceramic tradition with internet and crypto culture, using the vessel as social commentary. One side shows Pepe figures with guacamole labeled "BUY THE DIP," turning market slang into a literal joke. The reverse shows Pepes dancing outside a church, evoking belief and communal ritual akin to online and crypto spaces. Emerging from meme cultures like Reddit and Twitter, phrases like "buy the dip" operate as both humor and shared practice. These memes act as folk art for decentralized finance, turning volatility into identity and speculation into narrative. Barrows places ceramics within digital culture, highlighting how humor, volatility, and collective belief shape contemporary capitalism.

title: Trust the Process
description: Here, the meme becomes a meditation on belief: trust the process, commit to the journey, endure uncertainty. The phrase "TRUST THE PROCESS," hidden inside the rim, reads like a quiet mantra—meant to be held as much as seen. In crypto culture, this mirrors the HODL mentality: conviction through volatility, belief sustained through downturns, faith in an unseen outcome. The image of Pepe riding steadily through a sparse, otherworldly landscape suggests calm persistence rather than hype. Ceramics sharpen the contrast. The vessel is slow, fixed, and durable against the speed and instability of digital markets. In this tension, belief itself becomes material—shaped, fired, and made to endure even as everything else fluctuates.
